chapters.t: The Old House by the Sea
p: Nadia doesn't want to go to Grand-Bassam.

She says it in the car. She says it on the bridge over the lagoon. She says it again when they drive into the old town, past the big colonial houses with broken windows and trees growing on their roofs.
"Three weeks," she says. "Three whole weeks, with no friends, no network, no anything."
"Two months," says her mother, from the front seat. "Your father and I are in Dakar until the end of August. You know that."
"Two months!" Nadia falls back in her seat. "I'm going to die."
"You're not going to die," says her father, laughing. "Grand-Bassam is beautiful. Aunt Clémentine is wonderful. And the sea is the best medicine in the world."
Nadia puts her earphones in and turns up the music.

She is sixteen. She lives in a modern apartment in Cocody, with air conditioning, fast internet and a big window that looks at other big windows. All her friends are staying in Abidjan this summer. There are parties, there is the cinema, there is the new shopping centre. And she will be here, at the end of the world, with an old aunt she has seen maybe five times in her life.

Aunt Clémentine lives at the end of a sandy street, in a big yellow house with blue windows. The house is very old. The paint is falling off the walls in long, thin pieces, like the skin of a mango. But the garden is full of flowers: red bougainvillea, white frangipani, hibiscus as big as plates. And behind the house, behind a low wall, there is the sea.

Aunt Clémentine is waiting on the steps. She is about seventy, tall and thin, with short white hair, a long blue dress and a lot of silver bracelets that sing when she moves her arms. An enormous grey cat is sitting at her feet.
"Nadia! Look at you! The last time I saw you, you were this big." She shows a height near her knee. "And now you are a young woman."
She kisses Nadia on both cheeks. She smells of coconut oil and flowers.
"This is Monsieur," she says, pointing at the cat. "He is very old and very lazy, and he thinks he owns the house. Maybe he is right."
Monsieur looks at Nadia with yellow eyes, yawns, and goes back to sleep.

Her parents stay for one hour. They drink a coffee, they kiss her, they give her a lot of advice. Then their car disappears at the end of the sandy street, and Nadia is alone with an old woman, an old cat and an old house.
Her room is on the first floor. It has a big bed with a white mosquito net, an old wooden wardrobe, a small desk, and a door that opens onto a balcony.
Nadia goes out onto the balcony. And for a moment, she forgets to be angry.

The sea is right there. Huge and blue-green, with white waves that come and go, come and go, on a long beach of golden sand. Coconut palms lean over the water. Far away, a few fishing boats are coming back, painted in red, yellow and green. The wind is warm and salty. The sound of the waves is everywhere, like a big, slow heartbeat.
Then she looks at her phone. One bar of network. Then zero. Then one again.
She sighs. She sends a message to her best friend, Inès: *Help. I'm in prison. Prison with a view, but prison.* The message doesn't go.

That evening, they eat on the veranda: grilled fish, attiéké and a spicy tomato sauce. Aunt Clémentine talks about the house, about the old town, about her life. She was a French teacher in a high school in Bassam for thirty-five years. She never married. She has no children. "My students were my children," she says. "Three thousand children! It's enough for one life."
Then she looks at Nadia with her bright, intelligent eyes.
"You will be bored here, I know," she says with a smile. "Young people are always bored in Bassam at first."
"At first?"
"Yes. At first." Her silver bracelets sing. "And then, they never want to leave."
Later, Nadia sits on the balcony with her phone in her hand and nothing to do. The sun is going down, red and enormous, into the sea.
And down on the beach, alone on the sand, there is a boy sitting in front of a small wooden easel.
He is painting the sunset.
The next afternoon, Nadia is very bored.

She has read all the messages on her phone that arrived in the night. She has watched the cat sleep. She has helped Aunt Clémentine water the flowers. She has looked at the sea for a long time. It is beautiful, but you can't look at the sea all day.
"Go for a walk on the beach," says her aunt. "Take a hat. The sun is strong."
So Nadia takes a hat and goes down to the beach.

The sand is hot under her feet. The waves are big today, and they make a loud noise when they break. She walks along the water. There are a few fishermen repairing their nets, some children playing football, a woman selling coconuts from a wheelbarrow.
And there, near the old wooden boats, is the boy with the easel.
She doesn't want to look. But she is curious. She walks slowly, and she stops a few steps behind him.

He is painting the sea. But it is not the blue-green sea in front of them. In his painting, the sea is purple and gold, with waves of orange and pink, and a sky full of strange birds. It shouldn't look real. But somehow, it looks more alive than the real sea.
"You can come closer," says the boy, without turning around. "The sea doesn't bite."
Nadia jumps. "How did you know I was here?"
He laughs and points with his brush. "Your shadow is on my painting."
She looks down. It's true. Her shadow, with her big hat, is lying across the purple waves. She steps to the side, a little embarrassed.
The boy turns around. He is about seventeen, with short hair, bright eyes, and paint everywhere: on his fingers, on his old T-shirt, even a little blue on his nose.
"I'm Yann," he says.
"Nadia."
"You're the niece of Madame Clémentine. The girl from Abidjan."
"How do you know that?"
"Bassam is small. Everybody knows everything." He smiles. "Also, Madame Clémentine was my French teacher. She told everybody at the market that her niece was coming. She's very proud of you."
Nadia doesn't know what to say. Proud? Her aunt doesn't know her.
They talk. At first a little, then more.

Yann lives in Bassam all year, with his mother and his two little sisters. His mother sells attiéké at the market. His father died when he was ten. On Sundays, he sells his paintings to tourists near the old lighthouse.
"Do you sell many?"
"Sometimes. When the tourists are rich and a little crazy." He laughs. "Last month, a Frenchman bought three. I bought my mother a new gas cooker."
"And what do you want to do later?"
His face changes. It becomes serious. "I want to go to the École des Beaux-Arts in Abidjan. The big art school. I want to be a real painter. Not just for tourists. A painter people remember."
"So why don't you go?"

"Money," he says simply. "The school is expensive. Paint is expensive. Canvas is expensive. Life in Abidjan is expensive. And my mother needs me here." He looks at his painting. "There is a scholarship. A competition. Every year, they choose three young painters from all the country. But a lot of people try. A lot of people better than me."
"Nobody paints the sea like that," says Nadia. She means it.
Yann looks at her for a second, surprised. Then he smiles.
"And you?" he asks. "What do you love?"
Nadia opens her mouth. Then she closes it.
Nobody has ever asked her this question. Not her parents, who ask about her grades. Not her friends, who ask about boys and clothes. Not her teachers.
What does she love?
"I don't know," she says honestly. Then, very quietly: "Maybe writing. I write little poems. In a notebook. But I never show them to anybody."
"Why not?"
"Because they're bad. Because people will laugh."
Yann puts down his brush. He looks at the sea for a moment.

"Then show them to the sea first," he says. "The sea keeps all secrets. And it never laughs." He picks up his brush again. "Then, maybe, show them to me. I promise I won't laugh. I'm a painter. We are very serious people."
He has a big blue spot of paint on his nose. Nadia laughs. She can't stop.
The next morning, Yann is waiting in front of the yellow house with an old bicycle.
"Get on," he says. "I'm going to show you the real Bassam."
Nadia looks at the bicycle. It has no brakes and only one pedal. "Are you serious?"
"Very serious. I'm a painter, remember?"
Aunt Clémentine watches them from the window. She is smiling.

Grand-Bassam, Yann explains as he pedals, was the first capital of Côte d'Ivoire, more than one hundred years ago. In those days, it was a busy port, full of ships, merchants and big colonial houses. Then, in 1899, a terrible disease came — yellow fever — and many people died. The government moved the capital away. The merchants left. The houses stayed, empty, and slowly, the forest and the sea began to eat them.

"Today, the old town is protected by UNESCO," says Yann. "Like the pyramids in Egypt. We are world heritage." He laughs. "But nobody has money to repair the houses. So they're beautiful and they're falling down. Like old kings."

They ride past the old Governor's Palace, which is now the National Costume Museum. They ride past the old post office, the old courthouse, houses with tall windows and balconies of iron lace, where trees grow through the floors and goats sleep in the doorways.
Nadia takes photos with her phone. For the first time since she arrived, she forgets that there is no network.
They stop at the lighthouse. It is white and red and very tall. Yann knows the old guard, who lets them climb to the top. Two hundred steps. Nadia's legs burn.
But at the top, she stops breathing.

Everything is there, below them. On one side, the long beach and the endless sea, sparkling in the sun. On the other side, the calm green lagoon, with fishermen in pirogues and white birds. And between the two, the old town, with its red roofs, its yellow and pink walls, its coconut palms moving in the wind.
"Oh," says Nadia.
"Yes," says Yann. "Oh."
They stand there for a long time, in silence. It is a good silence.

At midday, Yann takes her to his house, in the new part of town. It is small, with a tin roof, and full of life. His mother, Madame Koné, is a big, warm woman with a loud laugh. His two little sisters, Grâce and Divine, are seven and nine, and they look at Nadia like she is a film star.
"Is she your girlfriend?" asks Divine.
"Divine!" Yann's face becomes very red.
"She's pretty," says Grâce.
"Both of you, go and play outside! Now!"
Madame Koné laughs so much that she has to sit down. She gives Nadia a big plate of attiéké with fried fish and chilli. It is the best attiéké Nadia has ever eaten.

After lunch, Yann shows her his room. It is tiny. There is a mattress on the floor, a small window, and paintings everywhere: on the walls, under the mattress, on the ceiling. The sea, the lagoon, the old houses, the fishermen, his mother at the market, his sisters asleep.
And many, many sunsets.
"Why so many sunsets?" asks Nadia.

Yann thinks. "My father was a fisherman. Every evening, at sunset, I went to the beach to wait for his boat. One evening, the boat didn't come back." He is quiet for a moment. "So now I paint the sunset. Every evening. It's my way of waiting for him. And my way of saying goodbye."
Nadia doesn't know what to say. So she doesn't say anything. She just looks at the paintings, one by one, slowly, the way you read a letter from someone you love.
When she leaves, she has the strange feeling that she knows Yann better than her friends of ten years.
That night, Nadia takes her notebook out of her bag.

It is a small green notebook, with a cover full of stickers. She has had it for two years. Inside, there are forty-three poems. Some are long, some are only three lines. Poems about the rain on her window in Cocody. About her grandmother, who died last year. About feeling alone in a room full of people.
Nobody has ever read them. Not one.

She goes down to the beach in the moonlight. The sand is cool now. The waves are softer than in the afternoon. She sits near the water, and, feeling a little stupid, she opens the notebook and reads a poem to the sea. Quietly. Then a second one, a little louder.
The sea doesn't laugh. It just comes and goes, comes and goes, as if it is listening.
*Show them to the sea first*, Yann said.
OK, she thinks. The sea, done. Now...
The next afternoon, on the beach, she gives the notebook to Yann.
"Don't read them now," she says quickly. "Read them later. When I'm not here. And if they're bad, don't tell me."
Yann takes the notebook very carefully, with his paint-covered fingers, as if it is made of glass.
The next day, he gives it back. He doesn't say anything for a long time. Nadia's heart is beating so hard she can hear it.
"So?" she says finally. "They're bad, aren't they?"
"Nadia." He shakes his head. "Your words are like my colours. You paint with words. That poem about the rain, the one with the blue umbrella — I read it ten times. Then I painted it."

He takes a small canvas out of his bag. It is a painting of a window, at night, with rain on the glass, and behind the rain, the lights of a city, blurry and gold. And at the bottom of the window, very small, a blue umbrella.
Nadia stares at it. Her own words, turned into colours.
Nobody has ever done anything like this for her.
"Keep it," says Yann. "It's yours. It was always yours. I just copied it."

On Sunday, Nadia goes with Yann to sell his paintings near the lighthouse. He puts them on a blanket on the ground: ten small paintings of the sea, the old houses, the fishermen. Tourists walk past. Some look. Most don't stop.
At midday, they have sold one painting. A small one, for five thousand francs.
"It's always like this," says Yann, trying to smile. "The tourists want cheap souvenirs. Not art."
Nadia looks at the paintings. Then she has an idea.
She takes her green notebook and some small white cards from her bag. For each painting, she writes a short poem — three or four lines — and she puts the card next to it.
Next to the purple sunset: *The sun goes down to sleep in the sea. / It leaves its gold for you and me.*
Next to the fishermen: *Strong hands, old boats, / Every morning, the sea says yes. / Every evening, the sea says maybe.*
Next to the old house with trees in the windows: *Once, kings slept here. / Now, the trees do.*

In the afternoon, something changes. People stop. They read the cards. They smile. They look at the paintings longer. A Ghanaian couple buys the fishermen. An old French lady buys the old house and asks if she can keep the card. A group of students from Abidjan buy two sunsets and take photos of the cards for Instagram.
At six o'clock, there are no more paintings on the blanket.
Yann counts the money with shaking hands. "Seventy-five thousand francs," he says. "Seventy-five thousand. In one day. Nadia, I never sold more than twenty thousand in one day."
"It's your paintings," says Nadia. "They're beautiful."
"It's your words," says Yann. "Together, they're... more."
They look at each other. Then they look away, quickly, both of them a little red. The sun is going down into the sea, purple and gold, exactly like in Yann's paintings.
That evening, Yann puts half the money in an envelope and gives it to Nadia.
"No," she says. "Keep it. For the art school. For the competition."
"Then it's an investment," he says. "When I'm a famous painter, I'll pay you back with interest. And I'll put your poems in my exhibition."
"Promise?"
"Promise."
July turns into August, and the days pass faster and faster.

Every morning, Nadia helps her aunt in the garden. Aunt Clémentine teaches her the names of all the flowers, and which ones the bees like, and which ones open only at night. They drink tea on the veranda. Monsieur the cat sleeps on Nadia's feet now. "He has adopted you," says her aunt. "That's a great honour. He has adopted only three people in twelve years."
Every afternoon, Nadia goes to the beach.

Yann shows her all his secret places. A small island in the lagoon where hundreds of white birds sleep. The place where the fishermen bring their boats at six o'clock, singing, and the whole village comes to help pull them onto the sand. An old abandoned hotel near the sea, with a swimming pool full of sand and frogs, where Yann painted his first painting when he was twelve.
Nadia reads him her new poems. She is writing a lot now: a poem every day, sometimes two. At first, she reads very quietly, looking at the sand. Then, slowly, with a stronger voice, looking at him.
He paints while she reads. Sometimes, he paints what she reads. Sometimes, he paints her.
One evening, they sit on the sand until the stars come out. There are millions of them here, far from the lights of Abidjan. The Milky Way crosses the sky like a river of milk.
They talk about everything. Their dreams, their fears, their families.
Nadia tells him about her parents. "They love me, I know. But they're always working. Always travelling. When they're home, they ask about my grades, my exams, my future. Never about... me."
"What do you want to tell them?"
She thinks. "That I don't want to be a lawyer, like my father. Or a banker, like my mother. That I want to write. Books. Poems. Stories." She laughs a little. "They'll say it's not a real job."
"My mother says painting is not a real job either," says Yann. "But she buys me paint with her attiéké money. Every month. Even when there's not enough money for meat."
They are quiet for a while.
"What are you afraid of?" asks Nadia.

Yann looks at the sea. "The sea," he says finally. "I love it, and I'm afraid of it. It took my father. Every time I paint it, I'm a little bit angry with it. And a little bit in love with it." He turns to her. "And you?"
Nadia thinks for a long time.
"I'm afraid that this summer will end," she says, very quietly. "And that I'll go back to Abidjan, and everything will be grey again. And I'll forget how this feels."
Yann doesn't answer. But very slowly, very carefully, he puts his hand next to hers on the sand. Their little fingers touch.
Neither of them moves. The waves come and go. The stars turn slowly over their heads.
Nadia has completely forgotten her phone. She has completely forgotten that she wanted to stay in Abidjan.
When she comes home that night, Aunt Clémentine is sitting on the balcony in the dark, with Monsieur on her knees.
"You're late," she says. She isn't angry. Her voice is soft.
"Sorry, Tantie. We were looking at the stars."
"I know. I saw you." Her aunt is silent for a moment. "He is a good boy, Yann. A very good boy. I taught him for three years. He has a big heart and a lot of talent."
"Yes," says Nadia.
Aunt Clémentine looks at the sea in the moonlight. Her bracelets are silent.
"Be careful, my dear," she says finally. "Summer loves are like waves. They come, and then they go. And sometimes, they take a part of you with them, and they never bring it back."
Nadia wants to ask what she means. But her aunt gets up, kisses her on the forehead, and goes inside.
Later, in bed, under the white mosquito net, Nadia thinks about her aunt's words. And about the strange sadness in her voice. As if she wasn't talking about Nadia at all.
In the middle of August, the sky changes.

In the morning, it is white and heavy. The air is so hot that nobody can breathe. The birds are quiet. The fishermen don't go out. They pull their boats far up on the sand and tie them to the coconut palms.
"A storm is coming," says Aunt Clémentine, looking at the sky. "A big one. Help me close the windows."

In the afternoon, the wind starts. First softly, then stronger, then so strong that the coconut palms bend like old men. The sea becomes grey and angry. The waves are enormous. They crash on the beach with a noise like thunder.
Then the rain comes. Not like rain in Abidjan. Like a wall of water falling from the sky.
At six o'clock, there is a terrible noise on the roof. Bang! Bang! Bang! Part of the old metal roof is moving in the wind, lifting, falling, lifting.
"The roof!" cries Aunt Clémentine. "If the wind takes it, the rain will come into the house! My books! My photos!"
She runs to the stairs. Nadia runs after her. But what can they do, an old woman and a sixteen-year-old girl, in a storm like this?
Then someone knocks on the front door. Hard.
Nadia opens it. It's Yann, completely wet, with a hammer, nails and a long rope.
"I saw your roof from the beach," he shouts over the noise of the wind. "Where is the ladder?"

For one hour, Yann works on the roof in the storm, with the rope tied around his waist and the other end tied to the balcony. Nadia holds the ladder and passes him the nails. Aunt Clémentine holds a torch and shouts instructions and prays at the same time. The rain is so loud that they can't hear each other. The wind tries to pull Yann off the roof three times.
But at seven o'clock, the roof is fixed.
Yann climbs down. He is shaking with cold. There is a cut on his hand. Aunt Clémentine puts a towel around his shoulders and pushes him into the kitchen.
"Sit. Tea. Now. And don't argue with your old teacher."

They sit in the kitchen while the storm screams outside. The electricity is cut, so there are candles everywhere. Aunt Clémentine makes tea with ginger and lemon. Monsieur the cat hides under the table.
Nadia cleans the cut on Yann's hand. He looks at her while she does it. She doesn't look up, but she can feel his eyes.
Aunt Clémentine watches them both. Then she gets up, goes to her room, and comes back with an old wooden box. She puts it on the table and opens it.

Inside, there are letters. Dozens of letters, yellow with age, tied with a faded pink ribbon. And on top, a black-and-white photo of a young woman with long hair, laughing on this same beach, next to a tall young man with a fisherman's cap.
"That's me," says Aunt Clémentine. "In the summer of 1974. I was seventeen."
"And the man?" asks Nadia.

"His name was Kwame. He was a fisherman from Ghana. He came to Bassam for one summer to work on the boats." She touches the photo with one finger. "He was the most beautiful man I ever saw. He sang all the time. He told me stories about Accra. We were in love, the way you can only be in love when you are seventeen."
"What happened?" asks Yann quietly.

"At the end of the summer, he went back to Ghana. He asked me to come with him. But my father said no. And I was afraid. Afraid of my father, afraid of a new country, afraid of everything. So I stayed."
She unties the pink ribbon.

"After he left, I wrote him a letter every week. For one year. Then every month. For ten years." She smiles a small, sad smile. "I never sent them. Not one. I was too proud. Or too afraid. I always thought: tomorrow. Tomorrow I will send them. And then it was too late."
Nobody speaks. Outside, the storm is calming. The rain is softer now.

"That's why I told you to be careful, Nadia," says her aunt. "Not because love is dangerous. Because fear is dangerous. If you love something — someone — don't wait. Don't write letters you never send."
She looks at Yann, then at Nadia.
"I waited fifty years. Don't be like me."

After the storm, everything is clean and bright. The sky is a perfect blue. The sea is calm again, as if nothing happened. On the beach, there are branches, coconuts and pieces of wood everywhere, and the children of Bassam run around collecting treasures.
But something has changed between Nadia and Yann. They don't say it. But they both know it.
Three days after the storm, Yann arrives at the yellow house running, with a piece of paper in his hand.
"It's open! The competition! The scholarship for the École des Beaux-Arts!"

He shows her the paper. Every year, the school chooses three young painters from all over Côte d'Ivoire. They get free classes for four years, a small room in Abidjan and money for paint. To apply, you must send three paintings and a letter explaining why you want to be an artist. The deadline is in two weeks.
"Two weeks!" says Nadia. "What paintings will you send?"

Yann's face becomes worried. "That's the problem. I don't know. I have hundreds of paintings. But are they good enough? Everybody who applies is good. Some of them have studied with real teachers. I learned alone, on the beach."
"That's why they're special," says Nadia.

They spend the next days choosing. They put all of Yann's paintings on the floor of his small room, on the bed, on the walls, in the courtyard. His sisters help. His mother gives her opinion, which is always: "All of them! They are all beautiful!"
Finally, they choose three.
The first is the purple and gold sunset, the one Yann was painting the first day Nadia saw him.
The second is his mother at the market, with her big pot of attiéké, laughing, with the sun behind her.

The third one is a new one. Yann painted it after the storm, in two nights, without sleeping. It is a girl on a balcony, reading from a small green notebook, in front of a sea that is purple and gold and silver. Her face is not very clear. But the way she holds the notebook — carefully, a little afraid, a little proud — is exactly right.
"That's me," says Nadia quietly.
"That's you," says Yann. "Is that OK?"
Nadia can't speak. She only nods.
Then there is the letter.
Yann sits at Aunt Clémentine's desk for hours. He writes, crosses out, writes again. He throws ten pages on the floor.
"I can't do it," he says finally, holding his head. "I can paint anything. But I can't write. Words don't obey me."
Nadia sits next to him. "Then tell me. Don't write. Just tell me why you paint."

So he tells her. About his father, and the boat that didn't come back. About the sunsets, every evening, to wait and to say goodbye. About his mother buying paint with attiéké money. About wanting to show the world that beauty doesn't live only in big cities and rich houses. That it lives in old falling houses, and tired fishermen, and women at the market, and in the sea that gives and takes.
Nadia writes it all down. She changes almost nothing. She just puts his words in order, like flowers in a vase.
When she reads it back to him, Yann's eyes are wet.
"Is that really me?" he asks.
"That's really you," says Nadia.
Aunt Clémentine, who is listening from the door, wipes her eyes with the corner of her blue dress, and pretends it's the dust.
The next morning, they go to the post office in the old town. Yann holds the big envelope with the three paintings and the letter against his chest like a baby.
"What if they say no?" he says.
"Then you try again next year," says Nadia. "And the year after. Painters are very serious people, remember? Serious people don't give up."
He laughs. He gives the envelope to the woman at the post office. She puts a stamp on it — bang — and drops it in a big bag.
It's gone.
They walk out into the sunshine. Without thinking, Yann takes Nadia's hand. This time, it isn't only their little fingers. It's their whole hands.
They walk back to the beach like that, and they don't let go.
The summer ends too fast.
On the last evening of August, Nadia's mother calls. "We are back from Dakar! We'll come and get you tomorrow morning at ten o'clock. Pack your bags, my darling. You must be so happy to come home!"
"Yes, Maman," says Nadia. Her voice is very small.
She puts down the phone and looks at the sea from the balcony. Tomorrow. Ten o'clock. It's impossible. She just arrived. She just started to live.

That evening, Yann can't come to the beach. His mother is sick — a fever since the morning — and he has to stay with his sisters and run to the pharmacy. He sends a message: *Sorry. Maman is sick. I'll come tomorrow morning, early, before you leave. I promise. The flat rock by the lighthouse, at eight.*
Nadia reads the message twenty times.
All night, she can't sleep. She sits at the little desk in her room, under the light of a candle, and she writes. Not a poem this time. A letter.

She writes everything she feels. That he is the first person who really saw her. That the day he read her poems and painted the blue umbrella, she felt like a real writer for the first time. That she doesn't want to forget this summer. That she doesn't want to forget him.
That maybe, maybe, this is what people call love.
She writes four pages. She doesn't cross out anything. At four o'clock in the morning, she folds the letter, puts it in an envelope, and writes on it: *For Yann. To keep. Not to sell!*
Then she thinks of Aunt Clémentine's wooden box, full of letters she never sent.
*Not me*, she thinks. *I'm going to give it to him. Today.*

At seven o'clock, she is already at the beach, at the flat rock near the lighthouse. The sun is rising behind the coconut palms. The fishermen are going out to sea. The beach is fresh and pink and quiet.
She waits.
Eight o'clock. No Yann.
Half past eight. No Yann. She sends a message. It doesn't go: no network. She sends it again. Nothing.
Nine o'clock. She walks up and down the beach, looking in every direction. No easel. No old bicycle with one pedal. No boy with paint on his nose.
Half past nine. Her eyes are burning. *He promised*, she thinks. *He promised.*
At a quarter to ten, she hears a car horn from the street. She turns around. Her parents' big grey car is stopping in front of the yellow house.
She walks back very slowly. Her mother gets out of the car and hugs her. "Look at you! You're so brown! You look so healthy! Did you have a nice time?"
"Yes, Maman," says Nadia.
Her father puts her bag in the car. Aunt Clémentine is standing on the steps with Monsieur the cat in her arms. She looks at Nadia's face, and she understands immediately.
Nadia gives her the envelope.
"Tantie," she says quietly, so her parents can't hear. "If you see him... please. Give him this. Please."
Aunt Clémentine takes the envelope with both hands, as if it is something very fragile. She looks at it for a moment. Then she looks into Nadia's eyes.
"I promise," she says. "This letter will not stay in a box. Not this one."
She hugs Nadia very hard. Her bracelets sing one last time.
"Come back, my dear," she whispers. "Bassam is your home now too."
In the car, Nadia doesn't speak.

Her mother talks about Dakar, about the hotel, about the meetings. Her father talks about the traffic. Nadia looks out of the window. She looks at the old houses with trees in their windows. The lighthouse, white and red. The long golden beach. The sea.
She looks at the sea until it disappears behind the lagoon, behind the bridge, behind the buildings of Abidjan.
And then she looks at nothing at all.
Back in Abidjan, everything is the same. And nothing is the same.

The apartment in Cocody is the same, with its air conditioning and its big window looking at other big windows. School starts again, the same school, the same uniform, the same teachers. Her friends are the same. Inès talks about a boy from the cinema. The others talk about parties, clothes, a new phone.
Nadia listens and smiles and says "Really?" at the right moments. But she feels like she is behind a window too. A window with rain on it.
There is no message from Yann.
The first week, she checks her phone every five minutes. Then every hour. Then every evening, before she sleeps. Nothing. His number doesn't answer. Her messages stay grey, not delivered.
"Maybe his phone is broken," says Inès, when Nadia finally tells her everything. "Or maybe he's just... a summer boy. You know. Summer boys disappear in September. It's normal."
"He's not a summer boy," says Nadia.
But at night, alone in her room, she isn't sure anymore. Maybe Aunt Clémentine was right. Summer loves are like waves. They come, and then they go.
She calls her aunt every Sunday. Aunt Clémentine talks about the garden, about Monsieur the cat, about the rain. Once, Nadia asks: "Tantie... did you give him the letter?"
There is a short silence on the phone.
"I keep my promises, my dear," says her aunt. "Have patience."
That's all she says. And Nadia is too proud to ask again.
But something else happens in those grey months. Something she doesn't expect.
She writes.

She writes more than ever before. Every evening after her homework, she sits at her desk and fills pages and pages. Poems about the sea. About the old houses. About the fishermen pulling their boats at six o'clock. About a boy painting sunsets to say goodbye to his father. About an old woman with a box of letters she never sent.
She fills the green notebook. She buys a second one, blue. Then a third, yellow like her aunt's house.

One day in October, her French teacher, Madame Bamba, reads one of her poems in class. It's for an exercise: *Write about a place you love.* Nadia wrote about Grand-Bassam. When Madame Bamba finishes reading, the class is silent. Then a boy at the back starts to clap. Then everybody.
After class, Madame Bamba keeps Nadia for a minute.
"There is a national poetry competition for young writers," she says. "The prize is publication in a real book, with other young poets. I think you should send something."
Nadia looks at her. "Me? Really?"
"You. Really." Madame Bamba smiles. "You have a gift, Nadia. Don't keep it in a notebook."

So Nadia sends five poems to the competition. The one about the blue umbrella. The one about the old houses. The one about the sunsets. The one about the fishermen. And a new one, the last one she wrote, called *Letters in a Box*.
Then, one evening at dinner, she does something even more difficult. She tells her parents.
"I don't want to be a lawyer," she says. "Or a banker. I want to write."
Her father puts down his fork. Her mother opens her mouth.
Nadia doesn't wait for them to speak. She gives them the yellow notebook. "Read this first. Please. Then you can say what you want."
Her parents read in silence for a long time. Her mother reads one poem twice. Her father takes off his glasses and cleans them, even though they are clean.
"Where did you learn to write like this?" asks her mother finally, very quietly.
Nadia thinks about the beach, the stars, a boy with blue paint on his nose, an old woman with silver bracelets.
"In Bassam," she says.
In February, six months after the summer, Aunt Clémentine calls on a Saturday morning. Her voice sounds strange: excited, like a young girl's.
"Nadia. Listen to me. Today, at four o'clock, go to the Plateau. To the new art gallery, the Galerie du Lagon, next to the cathedral. Today. Don't ask any questions."
"Tantie, what—"
"No questions! Four o'clock! And wear something nice." She hangs up.

At four o'clock, Nadia is in front of the Galerie du Lagon. It is a big white building with glass windows. There are a lot of people outside: elegant people with glasses of juice, photographers, students. On the door, there is a big sign:
**YOUNG PAINTERS OF CÔTE D'IVOIRE — École des Beaux-Arts — Exhibition of the New Scholarship Students**
Nadia's heart stops.

She goes in. The room is full of light and paintings and voices. She walks slowly from one wall to another. Paintings of cities, of forests, of faces. All beautiful. But she isn't looking at them. She's looking for something else.
And then she sees it.
In the middle of the room, on a white wall, alone, there is a big painting. A girl on a balcony, reading from a small green notebook, in front of a purple and gold and silver sea.
Next to it, there are two smaller paintings: a purple sunset, and a woman laughing at the market with a big pot of attiéké.
And under each painting, there is a small white card with a short poem. Her poems. Her handwriting, copied carefully in paint.
Under the big painting, there is another card:
*"Nadia" — Yann Koné. Scholarship student, École des Beaux-Arts. Poems by Nadia Achi.*
"I got the scholarship," says a voice behind her. "One of three in the whole country."
Nadia turns around.
Yann is there. He is wearing a white shirt that is too big for him, and new shoes that he clearly hates. But he still has paint on his fingers. And a little bit of blue on his ear.

"Your aunt gave me your letter," he says. "The same morning. At eleven o'clock. One hour after you left." He takes the envelope out of his shirt pocket. It's soft and old now, like a piece of cloth. "I've read it a hundred times. Maybe two hundred."
"Where were you?" Nadia's voice is shaking. "That morning. You promised. I waited for two hours."

"At the hospital," says Yann. "My mother. In the night, her fever was very high. At five in the morning, she couldn't breathe. A neighbour drove us to the hospital in Bassam. I stayed with her until midday. My phone was dead. No battery, no money for credit. I ran to the beach at eleven. You were gone."
He looks at the floor.
"She's OK now. It was malaria, a bad one. But she's OK. I'm sorry, Nadia. I'm so sorry I wasn't on the beach."
"And after? Why didn't you call? For six months!"

He looks embarrassed. "My phone was broken, really broken. And I didn't have your number written anywhere. Only in the phone. I asked your aunt. She said..." He smiles a little. "She said: 'Don't call her. Show her. Win that scholarship, then show her.' She's a very strict teacher, your aunt."
Nadia doesn't know if she wants to laugh or cry. So she does both, at the same time, in the middle of an art gallery full of elegant people.
Yann laughs too. And he takes her hand. And this time, they don't let go.
"You promised me something," she says, wiping her eyes. "On the beach. You said: when I'm a famous painter, I'll put your poems in my exhibition."
"I'm not famous yet," says Yann. "But I keep my promises too."
Behind them, someone is clapping slowly. They turn around.
It's Aunt Clémentine, in a long blue dress, with all her silver bracelets. And next to her, there is a very tall, very old man, with white hair, a straight back and a fisherman's cap in his hands.
"Nadia, Yann," says Aunt Clémentine. Her face is pink, like a girl of seventeen. "I want you to meet someone. This is Kwame. From Accra."
Nadia's mouth falls open.

"After you left," says her aunt, "I looked at that letter in my hands. Your letter. And I thought: if a girl of sixteen can be brave, an old woman of seventy can be brave too. So I opened my wooden box, and I sent all my letters to Ghana. All of them. Fifty years of letters, to an old address. I didn't think anyone would ever read them."
The old man smiles. He has a deep, warm voice, and he speaks English with a soft Ghanaian accent.
"I read them all," he says. "Every single one. It took me three weeks." He looks at Aunt Clémentine. "I never married either. I was waiting for a letter."

That evening, the four of them eat grilled fish and attiéké in a small restaurant on the lagoon. Yann talks about his classes. Nadia tells them that her poems were chosen for the national book. Kwame sings an old Ghanaian song, and Aunt Clémentine sings with him, very badly, and everybody in the restaurant laughs and claps.
Later, on the balcony of the restaurant, Nadia looks at the lagoon in the moonlight. Yann is next to her, his hand in hers.
She thinks about what her aunt said, that first summer night.
*Summer loves are like waves. They come, and then they go.*
Aunt Clémentine was wrong, she thinks. Or maybe she was only half right.
Some waves go.
But some waves come back.
**THE END**

title: A Summer in Grand-Bassam
author: Léxi
desc: Nadia, 16 ans, passe l'été chez sa tante dans une vieille maison jaune de Grand-Bassam. Un garçon qui peint la mer, des poèmes cachés, une boîte de lettres jamais envoyées… Roman complet.
